messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo Reyes is a 35-year-old Mexican American musician, married, who presents for his first course of psychological treatment following a life-threatening road accident that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. He was driving home late at night after a performance when a commercial truck ran a red light at speed and struck the driver's side of his car. The impact was severe enough to spin the vehicle across two lanes and into a barrier. Mateo was conscious throughout, pinned briefly by the crumpled door, surrounded by broken glass and the hiss of the engine, the smell of something burning. He remembers a man's voice somewhere outside the window, and he remembers thinking, with a strange, flat certainty, that he was going to die there. He did not. He was extracted by emergency services, treated for a fractured clavicle, lacerations, and a mild traumatic brain injury, and discharged within a week. The truck driver was never cited. No charges were filed.

In the weeks that followed, Mateo noticed that when he tried to sit quietly with what had happened — to construct a clear account of that night for his wife, for the insurance process, for himself — the memory refused to cooperate. It did not arrive as a coherent story. It came instead in shards: the particular sound the glass made, the pressure against his left shoulder, a fragment of light from somewhere above him. When he tried to reach deliberately for the sequence of events, he found a kind of blankness where the narrative should have been, as though the night existed only as scattered debris rather than a through-line he could follow. He has come to feel that he is working with an incomplete picture, that something essential is missing from his own account of what happened to him, and this incompleteness disturbs him in ways he struggles to articulate.

What Mateo can articulate, with considerable force, is his conviction that what was done to him was profoundly unjust, and that the absence of any legal or institutional consequence has compounded that injustice into something that sits in his chest like a weight. He is certain that nothing has been made right and that nothing will be. Alongside this runs a fear he finds almost more troubling than the accident itself: he has become afraid of his own anger. There are moments — stuck in traffic, reading about the case online, lying awake — when he feels the rage rise in him so sharply that he genuinely believes he will not be able to contain it, that he will do something he cannot take back. He does not trust himself. He has come to see his life as fundamentally altered, not temporarily disrupted — as though the man who played music and drove home at night and made plans with his wife belongs to a version of his life that is now closed off.

To manage this, Mateo has arranged his days so that he is almost never alone. He books sessions with other musicians, accepts every social invitation, keeps the television on when he is home and his wife is out. He has stopped talking to anyone — including her — about the accident or anything connected to it, and he does not allow himself to think about it deliberately, redirecting his attention the moment it begins to drift toward that night. His schedule, once built around the solitary discipline of practice and composition, has become a social structure designed to keep his own mind at a distance. The consequence has been significant: the long hours of private work that his music requires have contracted sharply. He has missed two recording commitments in the past six months. His collaborators have noticed. His wife has noticed. She knows something is badly wrong, but she does not know what, because he has not told her.

What finally brought Mateo to seek help was a conversation with his wife two weeks ago in which she told him, quietly, that she felt she was living with someone she no longer recognised. He did not argue. He is most afraid, sitting in the intake room, that the anger he carries will eventually confirm his worst fears about himself. What he hopes for, though he says it haltingly, is to find his way back to the music — and to her.
